stories.headline: A Corridor Agreed, and Still No Ship
stories.dek: A week ago Iran and Oman said they had a deal on a "temporary route" through Hormuz. Read the small print then and it was a metered lane, mostly in Iranian water, that Tehran itself called less than a reopening; read it now and nothing has changed but the calendar. The talk moved the oil price. Seven days on, no hull has moved through the lane. The strait has been largely shut since February.

stories.headline: Meta Reopens the Door It Shut Last Week
stories.dek: Five days after shipping a closed coding agent, Meta released Muse Glimmer — a 30-billion-parameter model under Apache-2.0, on Hugging Face, that fits on a single consumer card. The lab that invented the open-weights movement, then abandoned it, has swung back. And the "open" flagship everyone actually waited for, Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Max, is still a promise you pay for by the token.

stories.kicker: Screen & Sound · The Album Nobody's Heard
stories.headline: Ninety-One, and Not a Single Listener Yet
stories.dek: On Friday Phoebe Bridgers releases Lost Weekend, an album the critics have already scored into the nineties — a Metacritic 91, one perfect hundred — which means the only number that finally matters, the audience's, does not exist. Elsewhere on the culture desk, the summer's tentpole quietly passed $1.6 billion and keeps holding.

stories.headline: A Full Treasury Meets a Promise Without a Price
stories.dek: The economy keeps handing Lawrence Wong room he has not yet spent. Second-quarter growth ran at 5.7%, the forecast upgrade lands this month, and June's exports jumped a fifth on the year — so the "major review" of family support he announced on National Day arrives at the Rally with money genuinely available. The question the fortnight settles is no longer whether Singapore can afford to deliver. It is whether it will.

stories.headline: A Record Run of Million-Dollar Flats, Inside a Falling Index
stories.dek: The headline that sells papers is the 491 HDB resale flats that crossed a million dollars in the second quarter, a record. The number under it is the one that matters: the resale index is roughly flat on the year for the first time since 2019, and private prices are splitting by region. For a multi-property owner, the story is not the record — it is where the softness is quietly concentrating, and it is not where the cameras point.

stories.headline: The 360 That Led the Watchlist Finally Goes on Sale
stories.dek: The Insta360 X6 has topped this desk's gear watch since June on the strength of two nearly one-inch sensors and an 8K/50 mode. On Tuesday it stops being a leak and becomes an order page — US$699 for the standard bundle, $769 with the essentials. What it still is not, on launch day, is a camera any independent lab has measured. For a buy-once buyer, that is the whole verdict: it looks like the class leader, and nobody has proven it yet.

stories.headline: Aman Plants Its First Flag in Mexico
stories.dek: Amanvari opened this month on Baja California Sur's East Cape, on the Sea of Cortez — eighteen casitas, each with its own heated pool, from about US$4,500 a night, all-in. It is the classic Aman bargain, stated plainly: near-total seclusion, a real drive from the Cabo everyone pictures, priced so you feel the distance. The product is the emptiness around it.

stories.kicker: The Family Desk · The Ban, Eight Months On
stories.headline: The World's First Under-16 Ban Barely Dented the Scrolling
stories.dek: Australia banned under-sixteens from social media last December — the first country to try it. Eight months in, its own regulator's data says more than eight in ten are still on the platforms, at about the same frequency as before, while parents' awareness of what their kids actually do has fallen. The lesson for a Singapore parent is not that bans fail. It is that a wall a child walks around can lower the guard that was doing the real work. General guidance, not medical advice.

stories.kicker: The Macro Desk · The Last Quiet Session
stories.headline: A Jobs Shock Reset the Path; Now the Book Waits on the Print
stories.dek: Friday's payrolls didn't miss — they went negative, and the market repriced September from a live hike to a probable hold in a single session. Monday was the last quiet tape before the test: Tuesday's inflation print, expected tame, decides whether the relief was the start of something or a trap. Market explanation, not investment advice.

stories.kicker: The Rabbit Hole · The Home Studio
stories.headline: The Studio Became an App You Already Own
stories.dek: Electronic music production is making finished records in a bedroom, on a laptop, with everything — the drums, the synths, the mixing — either software or a small stack of hardware feeding it. The gateway is a single loop that loops. Under it sits a decades-deep craft, a gear rabbit hole with no bottom, and the argument tearing the community apart right now: what to do about the AI that can master your track, split it back into stems, or write the whole thing for you.

stories.headline: The Longevity Move Might Be Less Protein
stories.dek: A new review pooling more than 350 studies argues that restricting dietary protein — and three amino acids in particular — reproduces most of the metabolic and lifespan benefit on its own. For a mid-40s lifter who has spent years being told to hit his protein, it is a deliberate provocation. It also runs straight into the muscle-loss problem it can't wish away. General guidance, not medical advice.

stories.headline: An October Crunch at Home, a September Squeeze in Japan
stories.dek: Two big nights and a first-ever sprint collide in Singapore this October; across the region, mid-to-late September stacks the Asian Games, a game show and a sumo basho into the same fortnight. Book the flights and the hotels before the calendars do.

stories.headline: The Loudest Thing in Java
stories.dek: In the second- and third-tier towns of East Java, teenagers are building truck-mounted walls of subwoofers worth more than the houses they shake — and turning them into a working-class entertainment economy that Jakarta neither owns nor understands. Six days before Indonesia's Independence Day, one city just banned it. When the FT writes it up, it will have been rattling windows for a decade.
